New Year's Day. And I can't stop thinking about work.

Not doing it—just running scenarios. What if that client doesn't renew? What if the invoice bounces? What if the algorithm changes tomorrow?

The freelancer brain has no off switch. It's always humming in the background.

This year, I'm trying something that sounds ridiculous: scheduled worry time.

30 minutes every morning. Write down every work concern. Make a plan if needed. Then close the notebook and move on.

Here's what I've learned after 7 years of freelancing:

Compartmentalizing isn't avoidance. It's survival.

The alternative? Low-grade anxiety that bleeds into everything—dinners, weekends, sleep.

Anyone else struggle with the always-on feeling? What's worked for you?

#RemoteWork #WorkLifeBalance

I audited every subscription I'm paying for yesterday.

The results were embarrassing.

Here's what I found:

- Two cloud storage services doing the exact same thing
- A project management tool I opened exactly 3 times
- Premium features I upgraded to and forgot about
- A domain for a project idea I never started

Total money wasted: $847 for the year.

Not huge. But not nothing either.

The fix took 45 minutes:

1. Cancelled duplicates
2. Downgraded to free tiers where possible
3. Set calendar reminders before annual renewals

The survivors: password manager, VPN, cloud storage (one of them), invoicing tool.

Everything else was nice-to-have that I never actually used.

How many subscriptions are you paying for that you forgot about?

First real work day of 2026.

My inbox: 847 unread emails.

Most were newsletters and promotional stuff. But buried in there were three actual client messages and one late payment notification I almost missed.

Spent the first two hours just sorting and deleting. The rest of the day? Catching up on what I missed.

Not productive in the traditional sense. But necessary.

Here's what this taught me:

A separate email for newsletters makes sense. Keep the main inbox for actual work only.

Anyone do this successfully? Seems like a lot of setup but might be worth the mental clarity.

The VPN comparison article is finally live.

3 months of testing. NordVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark, and 4 others. Different locations. Different use cases. Different times of day.

The results surprised me.

Marketing claims don't match reality in most cases.

The fastest VPN? Depends entirely on where you are and what server you're connecting to. Speed varied wildly—even within the same service.

But here's what actually matters:

- Connection stability (not just speed)
- Whether the kill switch actually works
- How annoying the app is to use daily

Nobody talks about these in reviews. They're hard to measure. But they determine whether you actually keep using the VPN.

Full breakdown available now.

Spent this morning actually cleaning my home office.

Not reorganizing. Actual cleaning.

Dusted the monitor. Wiped down the keyboard. Found crumbs in places crumbs shouldn't be.

45 minutes. That's it.

The mental difference? Immediate.

Less visual clutter = less mental clutter. At least for me.

But here's the bigger realization:

I'd been ignoring this for months.

Remote work means no cleaning crew. No office manager making sure things look presentable. Just you and your gradually declining standards.

My solution: Monthly desk cleaning sessions. 15 minutes. On the calendar. Non-negotiable.

Small things compound.

Password manager update: still the single best security investment you can make.

This week alone it saved me twice.

1. A site I forgot about got breached—had a unique password there. No domino effect.
2. Needed to log into an old account. Would have definitely forgotten the password otherwise.

The resistance usually comes from fear:

'What if the password manager gets hacked?'
'What if I forget my master password?'

Valid concerns. But the alternative—reusing passwords or keeping them in a notes app—is way worse.

The breach notification feature alone is worth it. Getting an alert that your credentials were exposed before you're actually compromised? Priceless.

My recommendation: 1Password or Bitwarden. Both solid. Pick one and actually use it.

I did the math on my coworking membership for 2026.

Monthly cost: $250
Times I went last month: 3
Cost per visit: $83

My home internet: $70/month
Coffee I make myself: basically free

The numbers don't lie.

I'm paying a premium for social interaction I'm barely using.

Part of me wants to keep it for the option. For the days when home feels claustrophobic. For the networking events I never attend.

But does it actually make me more productive?

Honestly? My best work happens at home. Early morning, before anyone else is awake. Just me and the laptop and complete silence.

Maybe coworking isn't for everyone. Maybe it's okay to admit that.

Canceling this month. Will miss the fancy coffee machine. Won't miss the $250 bill.

#RemoteWork #FreelanceLife

A client asked me for laptop recommendations yesterday.

Remembered how confusing this space is.

Every brand has twelve models with names like XPS 15 9530 vs XPS 15 9520 vs XPS 15 Plus. Marketing specs don't match real-world performance. 'All-day battery' means different things to different manufacturers.

Here's what actually matters for remote work:

- 16GB RAM minimum (non-negotiable in 2026)
- Good keyboard (you're typing 8 hours a day)
- Actual battery life over 6 hours (not claimed—actual)
- Decent webcam (you're on video calls constantly)
- Under 4 pounds if you travel

That's it. Everything else is nice-to-have.

Ignore gaming specs unless you're gaming. Ignore creator marketing unless you're editing video.

Match the tool to the job.

Full laptop guide updated for 2026.

My Sunday planning ritual is embarrassingly simple.

Look at the week ahead. Identify three most important things. Ignore everything else until those are done.

Sounds easy. Actually doing it? Hard.

The inbox is always screaming. Slack never stops. There's always some 'urgent' thing that feels important in the moment but isn't.

This week's three things:

1. Finish the hosting comparison article
2. Send two overdue invoices
3. Prep for Thursday's client call

That's it. Everything else is noise.

If someone messages about something not on the list? It waits.
New opportunity email? It waits.

Ruthless prioritization isn't rude. It's survival.

The alternative is doing a little of everything and finishing nothing.

Been there. Didn't work.

#Productivity #RemoteWork

The note-taking app debate is eternal.

Notion vs Obsidian vs Apple Notes vs Roam vs whatever launched this week.

Here's what I've learned after trying most of them:

The best note-taking app is the one you actually use.

Revolutionary insight, I know.

But seriously. People spend more time configuring their productivity system than actually being productive.

The elaborate databases. The perfect folder structure. The tagging taxonomy.

All of it is procrastination dressed up as organization.

My current system: Apple Notes for quick captures. Notion for project documentation.

Two apps. No plugins. No templates. Just words in boxes.

Works fine.

The goal isn't a beautiful system. The goal is finding information when you need it.

Simple search beats complex organization every time.

What's your note-taking setup?

Had a call scheduled for 6am my time today.

Client in a different timezone. Limited availability. Had to make it work.

Woke up at 5:30. Made coffee. Tried to sound human. Think I pulled it off.

The time zone challenge never fully goes away. You can set boundaries, but sometimes you flex.

The key: knowing when flexing is worth it.

This client? Long-term relationship. Good pay. Reasonable most of the time. Worth the early alarm.

That one-time prospect who wanted a call at midnight? Politely declined. Not worth it.

The rule I follow:

Flex for relationships, not transactions.

People who respect your time 95% of the time get grace when they need it.

People who consistently ask for inconvenient times don't respect you.

Simple filter.

Two-factor authentication probably saved my business this week.

Got an alert that someone tried logging into one of my accounts from a location I've never been.

They had the password—probably from some old breach.

But they didn't have my phone.

Login blocked. Account secure. Crisis avoided.

The few seconds it takes to enter a code? Nothing compared to hours of recovering a compromised account.

Set it up on everything:

1. Email first (master key to everything else)
2. Financial accounts
3. Work tools

Backup codes matter too. Print them. Store them somewhere safe.

Authentication apps over SMS when possible. SIM swapping is real.

This isn't paranoia. This is baseline for working online in 2026.

Productivity myth that needs to die:

More hours = more output.

I worked 12-hour days for a year once. Thought I was being productive.

Was actually just present.

The quality after hour 8 drops off a cliff. Creative thinking disappears. You're just pushing buttons.

Now I aim for 6 focused hours. Sometimes less.

The output is better. The ideas are sharper. The work is actually done instead of half-done and needing revision.

The hard part? Convincing yourself this is okay.

Hustle culture made us equate busyness with value. Being available at all hours = dedication.

It's all wrong.

Results matter. Hours don't.

Try cutting your work day by two hours for a week. See what actually changes.

Bet it's less than you think.

#Productivity #WorkLifeBalance

Webcam quality tip nobody talks about:

It's almost never about the camera.

The laptop webcam everyone complains about? It's fine. The problem is lighting.

Sit facing a window during the day. Your face is lit naturally. You look human.

Sit with the window behind you? You're a silhouette. Mysterious but unprofessional.

The expensive ring lights and softboxes? Solutions to a problem that windows solve for free.

Not always possible, I know. But before you spend $200 on camera equipment, try rearranging your desk.

My current setup:

- Desk faces north-facing window
- Natural light all day
- Laptop webcam

Looks better than when I had a ring light in a dark corner.

Sometimes the low-tech solution wins.

Invoice update from this morning:

Got paid for work I did in November.

That's 68 days. NET-30 was the agreement.

This is freelance life. You do the work on time. You deliver quality. You send professional invoices.

And then you wait. And follow up. And wait some more.

What I've learned:

1. Payment terms matter more than hourly rate. NET-15 at lower rate beats NET-60 at higher rate.
2. Big companies pay slow. Always. Build it into pricing.
3. Invoice immediately upon delivery. Every day you wait adds to the timeline.
4. Automated reminders help but don't solve the problem.

The real solution? Retainers and deposits for new clients.

Get something upfront before work begins. Changes everything.

Tried the Pomodoro Technique again this week.

25 minutes focused work. 5 minute break. Repeat.

The theory is solid. Brain needs rest. Time-boxing creates urgency. Breaks prevent burnout.

In practice?

The timer went off right when I got into flow. The breaks felt artificial. I kept ignoring the prompts and feeling guilty.

Maybe I'm doing it wrong. Or maybe some productivity systems just don't fit certain brains.

What works for me: longer uninterrupted blocks. 90 minutes to 2 hours. Then a real break—walk outside, make food, do something physical.

Not Pomodoro compliant but actually sustainable.

The lesson: try the popular methods but don't force them.

Your optimal work rhythm might not match the internet's favorite technique.

And that's fine.

Added a plant to my home office last week.

Small thing. Didn't expect it to matter.

It matters.

Something about having a living thing in the room changes the energy. Not in a mystical way—just visually.

There's green. There's life. It's not just screens and cables and empty coffee cups.

Taking care of it is a nice micro-break too. Check the soil. Water if needed. 30 seconds of doing something that isn't work.

The plant won't make you more productive in any measurable way. It won't optimize your workflow or increase output.

But it makes the space feel less like a productivity machine and more like a place where a human spends time.

That's worth something.

Low maintenance options: pothos, snake plant, ZZ plant. All survive neglect.

Trust me—I've tested this.

VPN feature that matters more than speed: the kill switch.

Here's why.

A VPN encrypts your traffic. Good. But what happens when the connection drops?

Most of the time, your device just switches back to regular connection. Your traffic is now exposed. You might not even notice.

A kill switch blocks all internet traffic if the VPN disconnects.

Seems drastic. That's the point.

Either you're protected or you're offline. No middle ground where you think you're protected but aren't.

Tested this across several VPNs. Some kill switches work great. Some are buggy. Some are buried in settings you'd never find.

It's the difference between theoretical security and actual security.

If you're using a VPN for privacy, make sure this feature exists and is turned on.

Friday afternoon. Closing the laptop at 2pm.

No guilt. No checking email later. Actually done for the week.

This used to feel impossible.

The freelancer brain says you should always be available. Always working. Always hustling. Rest is for people with real jobs.

I bought into that for years. Burned out twice. Started resenting work I used to love.

Now I protect rest time the way I protect client deadlines. It goes on the calendar. Non-negotiable.

Client needs something urgently at 3pm Friday? Monday it is.

Nobody has ever complained. Nobody has ever left because I take weekends.

The desperation for availability was entirely self-imposed.

If you're running ragged, this is your permission slip.

Close the laptop. The work will still be there Monday.

#WorkLifeBalance #FreelanceLife

Backing up files is one of those things everyone knows they should do.

And almost nobody does consistently. Until something breaks.

Lost a hard drive once. Years ago. Most of my freelance work from that period—gone. Client files, project documentation, personal projects. All of it.

Now I use the 3-2-1 rule:

- 3 copies of important files
- 2 different types of storage (local and cloud)
- 1 copy offsite

Sounds paranoid. Probably is. But the 20 minutes a week on backups has paid off multiple times.

Cloud outage? Local copies.
Laptop dies? Everything's in the cloud.
Both fail? Okay, never happened. But if it does, I'm ready.

Don't wait until you lose something.

Set it up now. Future you will be grateful.

Saturday morning and the laptop is tempting me from the other room.

There's always something I could be doing. An email I could respond to. An article I could tweak. A lead I could follow up on.

The freelancer brain never fully rests. It runs scenarios constantly.

What if I lose that client?
What if the invoice doesn't pay?
What if the algorithm changes?

The work feels like it's never done because it literally isn't. There's always more.

This is the trap.

You can work yourself into exhaustion chasing 'more' and still feel behind.

The only answer I've found: set boundaries and accept that things will be left undone.

Not everything is urgent. Most things can wait until Monday.

The business will survive a weekend. Probably.

Closing the laptop now. See you Monday, LinkedIn.

Noise canceling headphones remain the best remote work purchase I've made.

Not close.

Using them right now at a cafe playing music too loud.

Without headphones: this place would be unusable.
With headphones: barely notice the music. Just me and my thoughts.

The investment pays off every single day.

Tested the main options over the past year:

- Sony WH-1000XM5: best noise canceling
- Bose: most comfortable for long wear
- AirPods Max: Apple ecosystem (but overpriced)

All three are good. Can't go wrong.

The cheap ones? Save your money. The noise canceling on budget options is barely there.

This is one category where spending more actually matters.

Sunday evening planning is my least favorite activity that I refuse to skip.

Looking at the calendar. Identifying big priorities. Saying no to things preemptively.

Takes maybe 30 minutes. Sets up the entire week.

Without it, Monday starts reactive. You open your inbox and let emails dictate priorities. Someone else's urgency becomes your focus.

The week happens to you instead of you happening to the week.

With it, you start Monday knowing exactly what matters. The inbox can wait. First 2-3 hours go to the priorities you identified when your brain was clear.

Not everyone does weekly planning. That's fine.

But if your weeks feel chaotic and you're always behind, try it for a month.

Just 30 minutes every Sunday. See what changes.

#Productivity #RemoteWork

International payments as a freelancer are annoying.

Clients in different countries. Different currencies. Different platforms wanting their cut.

Took me years to optimize this. Here's what I've learned:

Wise beats PayPal on fees. Almost every transaction. Not even close.

PayPal: 3-4% plus currency conversion fees
Wise: maybe 0.5%

On a $5,000 invoice, that's $200 vs $25.

Payoneer is decent for certain marketplaces but not as good for direct transfers.

Bank wires work but fees are unpredictable.

My setup now:

- Wise for most international clients
- PayPal only if client insists
- Local bank for domestic work

The fee savings over a year are significant.

Not glamorous. But neither is leaving money on the table.

Monday morning and my internet went down. Not for an hour—for the whole morning.

The universe testing my backup plans.

Good news: I have a mobile hotspot with unlimited data. Used my phone. Slower, but functional.

Bad news: I almost didn't have this. Relied on home internet being reliable for years.

The one time it mattered, I would have been stuck.

Lesson learned. If you work remotely, you need backup internet:

- Phone hotspot at minimum
- Dedicated mobile hotspot if you can expense it
- Know the nearest cafe with good WiFi
- Have a friend's address for emergencies

Redundancy isn't paranoia. It's professionalism.

Clients don't care that your internet went down. They care that you missed the deadline.

Hot take: Project management tools are mostly about team coordination.

If you're working solo, you probably don't need most of their features.

Notion, ClickUp, Monday, Asana—they're built for teams. Multiple people tracking tasks. Assigning work. Commenting. Sending updates.

When it's just you?

Apple Notes works fine. A paper notebook works fine. Whatever simple system you'll actually use works fine.

I've seen solo freelancers spend hours setting up elaborate Notion databases for work that could be tracked on a sticky note.

It's not productivity. It's procrastination with a productivity aesthetic.

Use the simple tool until you genuinely outgrow it.

When you hire someone or take on complex projects, upgrade then. Not before.

Got a phishing email yesterday that almost fooled me.

It looked exactly like a real invoice from a service I actually use. Logo was right. Formatting was right. Even had a realistic invoice number.

The only tell? The sender domain.

Instead of company.com, it was company-invoices.com.

Easy to miss if you're moving fast. I nearly clicked the attachment.

What stopped me was habit:

Always check the sender. Always. Even if the email looks legitimate. Especially if it asks you to do something.

Phishing attempts get more sophisticated every year. AI makes convincing fakes easier.

Your only defense: healthy skepticism and basic verification.

- Check the sender
- Hover over links before clicking
- When in doubt, go directly to the website

Simple stuff that works.

Standing desk confession: I've been sitting more. A lot more.

The $400 standing desk has been at sitting height for weeks.

What happened?

First, it got cold. Standing feels worse in winter somehow.
Then I got lazy about switching.
Then it just became a regular desk that sometimes goes up.

Thinking about whether it was worth it.

For some people, absolutely. They stand half the day. Their back feels better.

For me? Jury's still out.

What actually helps my back more: getting up every hour and walking around. Movement breaks. Stretching.

The standing desk lets me change position, which is good. But it didn't solve the core problem of being sedentary.

If you're considering one, maybe try a converter first. Lower investment. Same flexibility.

Halfway through January.

Checked on my resolutions from two weeks ago.

Honest assessment:

- Writing habit: going okay. 3 articles done.
- Exercise routine: inconsistent.
- Meditation: lasted exactly 4 days.

This is normal. The motivation surge of January 1st doesn't last.

Systems beat motivation every time.

What I'm adjusting:

1. Exercise gets scheduled like a client meeting. Immovable.
2. Meditation pairs with morning coffee. Already happening anyway—just adding 5 minutes.
3. Writing was already a habit, so I'm just protecting morning blocks.

The goals that fail are usually missing a system.

Wanting to do something isn't a plan.

Having a specific time, place, and trigger—that's a plan.

Ran a time tracking experiment this week.

The uncomfortable truth: I spend about 4 hours a day on billable work.

Not 8. Not 6. Four.

The rest is meetings, email, admin, context switching, and honestly just thinking.

Before tracking, I would have guessed 6-7 hours.

The data says otherwise.

This isn't failure—it's reality.

Deep focused work is exhausting. Most people can only sustain 3-4 hours per day. The rest is necessary but lower intensity.

The insight changed how I think about pricing.

I was calculating hourly rate based on 8-hour days.

Reality: it should be based on 4 hours of real output.

If you're not tracking your time, try it for a week. Just observe. Don't optimize yet.

The data is illuminating. And slightly humbling.

Client asked why I charge what I charge.

Usually I hate this question. Feels like the start of a negotiation.

This time I answered honestly. Sent my expense breakdown.

- Software subscriptions: $150/month
- Health insurance: $600
- Retirement savings: $500
- Taxes: roughly 30%
- Equipment depreciation
- Professional development

The actual take-home from my 'high' hourly rate isn't what it looks like on the invoice.

They got quiet. Then said they didn't realize how much running an independent practice costs.

Not everyone will respond this way. Some will still negotiate down.

But for clients worth keeping, transparency builds respect. They understand you're running a business, not extracting maximum dollars.

Know your numbers. Be willing to share them when appropriate.

The monitor debate: two screens vs one ultrawide vs just a laptop.

Used all three extensively. Here's my take.

Two monitors: better for reference work. Documentation on one, code on another. But also more temptation. Easy to have Slack open 'just in case.'

One ultrawide: better for focus. One field of vision. Split-screen is more intentional. Feels cleaner.

Just the laptop: surprisingly fine for most work. Forces prioritization. You can only see one thing, so you actually focus on it.

I've done my best writing on a 13-inch screen.

My current setup: one 27-inch at home. Laptop only when traveling. Sold the second monitor.

The marginal benefit wasn't worth the visual clutter.

Match the setup to how you actually work, not how you think you should work.

Friday flex: finished everything important by noon.

The afternoon is for errands and rest. The laptop stays closed.

This used to make me feel guilty.

Freelance culture says you should always be working. Available time is billable time. Rest is for the weak.

All of that is wrong.

Some weeks you work 50 hours because that's what the project needs.

Other weeks you work 25 hours because you were efficient.

Punishing efficiency by forcing more work teaches your brain to work slowly.

I protect Friday afternoons now.

If everything important is done, the week is done.

Emails wait until Monday. Prospecting waits. The 'I should probably' tasks wait.

Rest is part of the system. Not what you do when you fail to find more work.

It's what keeps you sustainable for the long run.

Email marketing tools comparison is finally ready.

Tested ConvertKit, Mailchimp, Beehiiv, and Buttondown over the past few months.

The verdict: they all do essentially the same thing with different UI and pricing.

ConvertKit: best for creators who want automations. The visual builder is genuinely good.

Mailchimp: most familiar if you've been doing this for years. But free tier keeps shrinking and prices keep climbing.

Beehiiv: the new hotness for newsletters. Good growth features. Clean design.

Buttondown: simple and cheap. No frills. Just sends emails reliably.

For most people starting out: Buttondown is fine.

For complex funnels: ConvertKit.

For everyone else: whichever free trial you actually finish setting up.

The best tool is the one you'll actually use. Analysis paralysis is the real enemy.

Travel adapter tip from someone who's been caught without one:

Get the universal adapter. Carry it always.

Every time I've thought 'probably won't need it for this trip' I've needed it.

Different countries have different outlets. Even within regions there's variation.

The universal adapters with multiple plugs seem bulky but work everywhere. The ones with built-in USB ports are even better.

Current favorite: the flat ones that lay against the wall instead of sticking out. The sticking-out ones fall from loose outlets.

$15. Weighs nothing. Saves you from the airport scramble when your laptop is dying and your charger won't fit.

Throw it in your bag permanently. Forget about it.

Already anxious about everything that could go wrong.

Will the WiFi work? Will I find a quiet place for calls? What if my laptop dies?

Always fine. The catastrophes you imagine rarely happen.

Video call setup that works:

1. Good internet
2. Decent audio
3. Acceptable video

In that order. Prioritize accordingly.

Internet: everything depends on this. 25+ Mbps upload for smooth video. Test before important calls. Have a backup plan.

Audio: more important than video. People tolerate blurry video. They won't tolerate bad audio. A $50 USB microphone changes everything.

Video: laptop webcam is fine with good lighting. Face a window. That's the tip.

The elaborate setups with ring lights and green screens? Nice to have. Not necessary.

I've seen CEOs take calls from car front seats. As long as you're visible and audible, you're professional enough.

Content over production value. Every time.

Monday morning and there's no motivation. None.

The to-do list is long. Deadlines are real. And I'd rather do absolutely anything else.

This is normal.

Waiting for motivation is a trap. It doesn't come reliably. It's not coming this morning.

What works: start anyway.

Do the smallest possible version of the first task.

Motivation follows action, not the other way around.

The psychological trick is just beginning. Any beginning. Open the document. Write one sentence. The rest usually follows.

The days when motivation appears naturally are a gift. But you can't build a business on gifts.

The reliable thing is the system. Same time, same place, same routine.

Start whether you feel like it or not.

Closing the motivation waiting room now. Work begins.

VPN question I get asked more than any other:

Do you actually need one?

Honest answer: it depends.

Public WiFi? Yes. Coffee shops, airports, hotels—all attack surfaces. VPN encrypts your traffic.

Sensitive accounts on public networks? Definitely yes. Banking, client portals, anything with passwords.

Work from home on your own network? Less critical but still useful for privacy. Your ISP can see everything.

Travel internationally? Yes. For security and accessing services blocked in certain countries.

For most remote workers: probably yes.

The cost is minimal ($3-10/month). The protection is real. Peace of mind is worth something.

Better to have it and not need it than need it and not have it.

Tax season approaching.

The annual ritual of finding every receipt, cursing my past self, and wondering if that coffee was a business expense.

This year is better though.

Actually tracked expenses throughout the year. Most of them anyway. The app just exports a CSV. Receipts photographed and tagged. Accountant gets an organized folder instead of a shoebox.

Deductions I almost missed:

Home office: real money. Square footage calculation took 10 minutes. Portion of rent, utilities, internet.

Equipment: standing desk, monitor, laptop. All deductible.

Professional development: courses, conference tickets, industry books.

This is money the government isn't asking for. It's yours if you track it.

If you haven't done this for 2025, start now. Gather receipts. Do the math.

Future you will appreciate the refund.

The cables under my desk are a disaster.

There. I admitted it.

I have excellent cable management advice. I've written about it. And my own setup looks like a spaghetti monster lives under there.

The irony isn't lost on me.

What I tell people: velcro ties, cable trays, label everything, route along desk legs.

What I have: cables everywhere, tangled together, one mystery cord I'm afraid to unplug.

Two-factor authentication PSA since I've been talking about security:

Your backup codes matter as much as the main authentication.

Few minutes of setup prevents hours of account recovery hell.
